673.title: Faith and works (James 2:14–26)
673.hook: faith without works is dead; Luther found James hard, but all churches read it
673.howItsDone: Christians read James 2 alongside Paul's letters, and churches often pair Sunday worship with practical service, such as food banks, coat drives and visiting, as faith put to work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gold ring and the good seat, and your line was mercy triumphs over judgment. Who did you give the first word or the best seat to? Day six hundred seventy-three.

It's winter. A neighbor knocks on your door. No coat, and they haven't eaten since yesterday. You smile warmly and say, I'll be thinking of you. Stay warm. Eat something. Then you close the door. James paints exactly this scene, and asks one short question: what good is that? It's the setup for a paragraph Christians still argue over. Martin Luther found it hard going. And still, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles all keep it.

In the King James Bible: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?" Then the line everyone knows: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." A faith that only talks is like those warm words at the door. It sounds right and it changes nothing. James gets sharp: you believe there is one God? Good. "The devils also believe, and tremble." Knowing the right facts isn't the same as trusting with your life. Then two examples. Abraham, willing to offer Isaac. And Rahab, the woman in Jericho who hid Israel's spies and sent them out another way. A patriarch and an outsider. Faith showed itself in what each did. He ends: "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also." Here's why it's argued over. Paul wrote that a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law. James writes that a person is justified by works, and not by faith only. In his 1522 preface to the New Testament, Martin Luther called James a letter of straw, compared with books like Romans. He still kept it in his Bible. Christians read the two side by side differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often point to James when they teach that God's grace saves through a faith alive with love and good works. Protestant churches in Luther's line teach that people are saved by faith alone, and that real faith always gets up and does something, which is how they read James. James's own point is plain: a faith that never opens the door isn't what he means by faith.
screen: then, large: `FAITH, IF IT HATH NOT WORKS, IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one work that shows your faith, or simply what you love. Settle, and breathe. Think of one need you know about right now. Not the whole world's need. One. A neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a stranger you pass every day. Picture the warm words you might say to them. Then picture one thing your hands could actually do: a meal, a ride, a coat, an hour, a bill paid, a call made. Keep it small and real. Decide when you'll do it. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to follow through. The bell holds the time.
Works. James's test for living faith: faith without works is dead, the same way a body without breath is dead.
Your line: faith that works. Today, turn one nice word into one done thing, before the sun goes down. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: The tongue (James 3:1–12)
674.hook: a small rudder, a small spark: the tongue sets forests on fire
674.howItsDone: Some Christians include their speech in a daily or weekly self-examination, and churches turn to James 3 when teaching about gossip, anger and online behavior.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and works, and your line was faith that works. Which kind word did you turn into a done thing? Day six hundred seventy-four.

A wildfire can start from almost nothing. A spark from a dragged chain. One cigarette. A campfire left smoldering. A few days later the smoke is visible from space, and whole towns are packing their cars. Investigators sometimes trace the fire back to a single point on the ground, small enough to cover with your hand. James never saw a satellite photo, but he knew what a small fire can do. And he used it to describe something that sits in every mouth.

He starts with a warning to teachers. Not many of you should become teachers, he says, because teachers will be judged more strictly. People who talk for a living have more to answer for. Then three pictures of small things steering big ones. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A huge ship, driven by fierce winds, is "turned about with a very small helm," the rudder, wherever the pilot wants. And then the third: "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" That word matter in the King James is a bit of a puzzle in English. The Greek word means wood, or forest. How great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. The bit and the rudder steer. The spark destroys. Then James says something that stings: people have tamed every kind of animal, birds and snakes and sea creatures, "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." And here's the line that turns it inward. "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be." With the tongue, James says, we bless God, and with it we curse people made in God's likeness. Praise on Sunday, cursing by Monday. James asks: does a spring pour out fresh water and bitter from the same opening? Can a fig tree grow olives? He isn't saying never speak. He's saying words are fire. They can warm a house or burn it down, and the same mouth does both.
screen: then, large: `HOW GREAT A MATTER A LITTLE FIRE KINDLETH!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say no unkind word today. Settle, and breathe. Think back to the last unkind thing you said, out loud or in a text. Don't punish yourself; just look at it. Where did it go? Who heard it, and who did they tell? Picture it like a spark landing in dry grass. Now picture today. Where are you most likely to say something sharp? With whom? Picture that moment and your mouth staying closed, or opening with something else. A breath first. If you pray, you can ask for a guard on your mouth. The bell holds the time.
The tongue. For James, a small part of the body that steers like a rudder and burns like a spark, and that no one can fully tame.
Your line: a small fire. Today, before you send any message written in irritation, wait ten minutes, then reread it as the person getting it. Day six hundred seventy-four.

675.title: Wisdom from above (James 3:13–18)
675.hook: peaceable, gentle, easy to entreat, full of mercy
675.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to James 3:17 as a short list of what wise leadership looks like, and some churches use it when choosing leaders or working through a dispute.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tongue, and your line was a small fire. Did you hold back one message written in irritation? Day six hundred seventy-five.

Who is the wisest person you know? Not the smartest. Not the one with the most degrees or the quickest comeback. The wisest. Chances are you're picturing someone calm. Someone you could tell anything to. Someone who listens before answering and somehow leaves the room more peaceful than they found it. Cleverness wins arguments. But when people name someone wise, it's often someone gentle. James noticed the same thing. He asks the question straight out: who is wise among you? Then he describes two kinds of wisdom.

First, the test. If you're wise, James says, show it by a good life, by works done in "meekness of wisdom." Meekness isn't weakness. It's strength that doesn't need to shove. Then the first kind of wisdom, the kind that comes from below: full of bitter envy and selfish ambition. It may look clever. It may even win. But James is blunt about what it leaves behind: "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work." Confusion is disorder, things coming apart. Think of an office run on rivalry, or a family where everyone keeps score. Then the second kind. In the King James Bible: "But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy." Seven marks, and look at them. Not one is about being clever. Pure, meaning with no hidden motive. Peaceable. Gentle, the word means reasonable, yielding. And easy to be intreated, one word in Greek, which as far as we know appears only here in the New Testament. It means open to persuasion. Willing to be talked to. Willing to change your mind. Then full of mercy, without partiality, which echoes James's gold ring, and without hypocrisy, the same inside as outside. And he closes with a seed: "And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace." Peacemakers plant, and what grows is goodness. Wisdom from above isn't measured by how hard you win. It's measured by what grows after you leave.
screen: then, large: `THE WISDOM THAT IS FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be easy to talk to. Settle, and breathe. Think of the last time someone disagreed with you or tried to correct you. Remember how your body reacted. Tight jaw? Crossed arms? A reply already loading? Now picture the same moment, but this time you are easy to be intreated. Your shoulders drop. You ask, tell me more. You let them finish. You allow yourself to consider that they might be right. Stay in that picture for a while. Notice how it feels to hold an opinion loosely. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom from above. The bell holds the time.
Meekness. James's word for strength that doesn't need to shove: wisdom from above, pure, peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy.
Your line: gentle wisdom. Today, in one disagreement, ask one honest question before you make your own point. Day six hundred seventy-five.

676.title: Draw near to God (James 4:1–10)
676.hook: draw near to God and he will draw near to you
676.howItsDone: Some churches use James 4:8 as a call to worship or before a prayer of confession, especially in Lent, when worshipers are invited to come near to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wisdom from above, and your line was gentle wisdom. Did you ask an honest question before making your own point? Day six hundred seventy-six.

"From whence come wars and fightings among you?" That's how James opens chapter four, in the King James Bible, and he isn't talking about armies. He means the believers he's writing to. Members fighting with members. Arguments in the parking lot. Grudges that last for years. Where does all that come from? It's a fair question for any family, any office, any group chat that's gone quiet and cold. James's answer is uncomfortable, and then, a few lines later, it turns into a promise.

Here's his answer: "come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" The fight outside starts as a fight inside. You want something and don't have it, so you scheme and quarrel. And then a short line that stings: "ye have not, because ye ask not." Or, he adds, you ask with the wrong motives, just to spend it on your own pleasures. Then James quotes Proverbs: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." And here the letter turns. A string of short commands, almost like a drumbeat. "Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you." Draw nigh. Some readers hear a priestly word here: the old Greek translation of Exodus uses it for priests who come near to the Lord. If so, James hands that priestly word to everyone. And the promise has two sides. You take a step, and God takes a step. In James's picture, God isn't waiting at a distance with crossed arms. God comes toward you. Then James says what drawing near looks like: wash your hands, purify your hearts, you double minded. Let your laughter turn to mourning, he says, meaning take your wrongs seriously. Then the last line of the paragraph lifts everything back up: "Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up." The proud are resisted. The humble are lifted. The fights start inside, and so does the way back.
screen: `YE HAVE NOT, BECAUSE YE ASK NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step toward God, or toward the holy, as you understand it. Settle, and breathe. Picture a doorway, and you standing a few steps back from it. Notice what's kept you at a distance lately: busyness, a quarrel, shame, or just forgetting. Name it. Now, in your mind, take one step forward. Just one. You don't have to fix everything first. Then rest, and imagine the other side of the promise: the doorway coming closer to you too. If you pray, you can simply say, here I am. The bell holds the time.
Double minded. James's name for the proud and quarreling: told to purify their hearts and draw near to God, who then draws near to them.
Your line: draw near. Today, the next time you feel a fight rising inside, take one step back toward God, or toward stillness, before you speak. Day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: If the Lord wills (James 4:11–17)
677.hook: you are a mist that appears for a little while
677.howItsDone: Some Christians add "God willing" or "Lord willing" when speaking of future plans, and some still write D.V., for Deo volente, at the end of a letter or a notice of meetings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, draw near to God, and your line was draw near. When a fight rose inside you, did you take a step back toward stillness first? Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Open your calendar app. Look at next month. There it is, all laid out in neat colored blocks: the trip, the deadline, the dentist, the dinner. It looks so certain on the screen. Now think back to a year ago. How much of what you planned then actually happened the way you planned it? James turns to people making plans like that: traders off to a city for a year to buy and sell. And he speaks to them in a voice that sounds like he's reading over their shoulder as they plan.

First a quick word against speaking evil of one another: there is one judge, he says, so who are you to judge your neighbor? Then the business plan. In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain." Today or tomorrow. Such a city. A year. Profit. It's very specific, and very confident. Then James says: "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." A vapor. The breath you see on a cold morning. The steam off a cup of coffee. The mist on a field at dawn that's gone by nine. It's there, it's real, and then it isn't. James doesn't say, so don't plan. He gives them better words for planning: "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that." Make the plan. Hold it with an open hand. The phrase passed into Christian speech. Some still write the Latin letters D.V., Deo volente, God willing, at the bottom of a letter about future plans. Muslims say something close, in sha' Allah, if God wills, and Jews say im yirtzeh Hashem. It's a shared human humility about tomorrow. And the passage ends with a line that turns the whole thing around: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin." If life is a vapor, the good you know you could do is for today. Not someday.

Here's the practice: plan loosely today. Settle, and breathe. Picture your plans for the rest of today and tomorrow, block by block. Now imagine each one written on a little card, and you holding the cards in an open hand instead of a fist. Feel the difference in your hand. Notice which plan you're gripping hardest. Breathe out slowly, and watch your breath disappear, the way James's vapor does. Then think of one good thing you know you could do today and have been putting off. If you pray, you can offer your plans to God. The bell holds the time.
Vapor. James's picture for a life that's here today and gone tomorrow: the breath you see on a cold morning, real, and then gone.
Your line: a little while. Today, do the one good thing you've been saving for someday, while it's still today. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Wages held back (James 5:1–6)
678.hook: the wages you withheld cry out
678.howItsDone: Some churches draw on James 5 and Deuteronomy 24 in their teaching on fair wages and workers' rights, and some congregations make a point of paying their own staff and contractors promptly and fairly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the Lord wills, and your line was a little while. Which good thing did you stop saving for someday? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Sundown at the edge of a harvested field. The reapers have been cutting grain since morning, and now they wait for the day's pay. No savings account. No paycheck next Friday. The old law of Moses says why that pay can't wait: the worker is poor, and has set his heart on it. Tonight the owner says, come back next week. That's the scene behind today's passage. And James, who has been practical and plainspoken for four chapters, suddenly raises his voice.

In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you." It sounds like the old prophets, Amos or Isaiah, thundering against injustice. Then pictures of wealth rotting where it's stored: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten." The gold and silver, he says, have rusted, and the rust will be a witness against you. Hoarded things decay. Then the heart of it: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth." The wages themselves cry out. Money that should have been in a worker's hand has a voice. And it reaches God. Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer his wage on the same day, before the sun goes down, so that he doesn't cry to the Lord against you. James is drawing on that old command. And notice the title he uses for God. Lord of sabaoth. It isn't sabbath. It's a Hebrew word meaning armies, or hosts. The Lord of hosts. The commander of heaven's armies is listening to the cry of a farmhand who wasn't paid. Some churches teach from this passage that a fair wage, paid on time, isn't charity. It's justice.
screen: then, large: `KEPT BACK BY FRAUD, CRIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay someone promptly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work you depend on that you rarely see. The person who picks your fruit. Who cleans the office at night. Who delivers the packages. Who sews the clothes you're wearing. Picture one of them. Then think closer to home: do you owe anyone right now? An invoice, a babysitter, a friend who covered lunch, a bill you've let slide. Name it. Decide when you'll pay. If you pray, you can pray for workers who are waiting on wages. The bell holds the time.
Sabaoth. Hebrew for hosts, armies, the Lord of hosts: the title James uses when he says a worker's unpaid wages cry out and reach God's ears.
Your line: the wages cry out. Today, pay one thing you owe, a bill, a loan, a babysitter, sooner than you have to. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: The patient farmer (James 5:7–12)
679.hook: the farmer waits for the early and late rain
679.howItsDone: James 5:7–10 is an Advent reading in some church lectionaries, in the season of waiting before Christmas, and Christians often turn to it in long illnesses or hard seasons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wages held back, and your line was the wages cry out. Which bill or debt did you pay sooner than you had to? Day six hundred seventy-nine.

You can't make a seed grow faster by yelling at it. Anyone who has kept a garden knows this. You plant. You water. Then you wait, and the waiting is most of the work. The Bible speaks of two rains in that land, the early rain and the latter rain. Commentators place the early one in autumn, softening hard ground for plowing and sowing, and the latter in spring, swelling the grain before harvest. Between them, months of watching the sky. James has just thundered at the rich who cheated their workers. Now he turns to his brethren, people waiting for things to be put right, and gives them a farmer to look at.

In the King James Bible: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." Husbandman is the old word for farmer. And the patience he has isn't passive. A farmer's waiting isn't idle. Farmers weed and mend fences and fix the plow. But they can't make it rain. They work hard on what they can do, and they wait for what they can't. Be patient like that, James says, and steady your hearts, because the coming of the Lord is near. Then a practical warning for people under strain: "Grudge not one against another." When people wait a long time, they turn on each other. Look, the judge is standing at the door. Then James offers two more pictures of endurance. The prophets, who spoke for God and suffered for it. And then: "Ye have heard of the patience of Job." Patient as Job, people say. Yet in the book of Job, he doesn't sit quietly. He argues, he laments, he demands an answer from God. The Greek word James uses here means endurance, staying under the weight, and that is exactly what Job did. He complained loudly, and he didn't let go. And James says, you've seen how it ended: the Lord is full of pity and mercy. Last, a quick word about honesty: don't swear oaths. "Let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." When you're waiting on God, keep your word plain. This week has been one long walk through James: faith and works, the tongue, wisdom from above, draw near, if the Lord wills, wages held back, and now the patient farmer.
screen: `JOB: LOUD, BUT HE DIDN'T LET GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're waiting on right now. A test result, a reply, a change in someone you love, a door that hasn't opened. Name it. Then sort it in two piles, like a farmer. What part of this can I work on? And what part is rain, out of my hands? Picture setting the rain part down. Then breathe into the waiting itself, without trying to hurry it. Notice if you feel any grudge rising toward someone in the waiting. If you pray, you can ask for patience. The bell holds the time.
Job. The example James gives of patience that still argues and laments loudly, enduring under the weight without letting go of God.
Your line: be patient. Today, when you catch yourself refreshing, checking or pushing on the thing you're waiting for, do one useful thing within your reach instead. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
